arguments.text: Benchmark sources report: Rewards for Justice describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service group targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. It says online aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, and Dandis are believed linked to Conti, and lists associated location Russia, organization Conti/Wizard Spider, and applications Conti RaaS, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. RFJ says Conti was first detected in 2019, used in more than 1,000 operations, and victimized more than 400 organizations worldwide, over 290 in the U.S.; these are government-site assertions. CIS explains RaaS as developers leasing malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits, often 70/30, and describes Conti double extortion, ties to TrickBot, internal leaks after the February 2022 Ukraine invasion, business units, distinct roles (Coders, Testers, Administrators, Reverse Engineers, Penetration Testers/Hackers), outsourced spamming, separate budgets, and an insider estimate of more than 60 employees in July 2021. CIS reports post-leak dismantling/rebranding into smaller units and later shutdown of leak and negotiation infrastructure. Rapid7 reports the Feb. 27 2022 ContiLeaks disclosure of 14 MB across 393 JSON files, some encrypted and incomplete; chats, screenshots, tools, exploits, design processes, credentials and alleged server details were leaked. Rapid7 assesses the leaker was likely a senior member or disgruntled affiliates, and describes interviews, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product development, phishing, endpoint-evasion testing, a control panel, and well-organized/funded operations; it reports an alleged FSB funding conversation but no independent verification in the text. DOJ identifies defendants Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov in case 3:23-CR-00092, charged in Sept. 2023 with CFAA and wire-fraud conspiracy for roles in the Conti ransomware conspiracy; Oleksii Lytvynenko in case 3:23-CR-00088, charged in Nov. 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti and later pleaded guilty to Count 2 conspiracy to commit wire fraud in June 2026. DOJ explicitly says defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. The benchmark search results did not establish any mapping between these named defendants and the RFJ aliases; do not infer one.

# Final Report: Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive summary

Public sources describe Conti as a large, commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, also known as Wizard Spider. The reported model separated malware development and operational support from victim intrusions conducted by affiliates, with profits shared between the operators and affiliates. Conti reportedly used double extortion: stealing and encrypting victim data, then threatening publication or sale if ransom demands were not paid. [SRC-001][SRC-003]

The 2022 ContiLeaks disclosures exposed internal communications, operational tools, credentials, infrastructure details, and discussions of recruitment, salaries, software development, phishing, and evasion. The material was incomplete because some files were encrypted, and Rapid7 characterized the identity of the leaker as uncertain. Nevertheless, the leaks were assessed as showing an organization with distinct technical and administrative functions and substantial resources. [SRC-002][SRC-003]

U.S. government records publicly associate the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” with Conti, and identify Wizard Spider as another name for Conti. The same records do not establish which, if any, of those aliases correspond to the defendants named in the Department of Justice cases. DOJ records separately identify five defendants charged in Conti-related conspiracies; one later pleaded guilty to a wire-fraud conspiracy count. The charges and allegations should not be treated as proof against defendants who remain entitled to the presumption of innocence. [SRC-001][SRC-004]

---

## 1. How public sources describe Conti as an RaaS operation

### Organizational and commercial model

The Center for Internet Security describes RaaS as a model in which ransomware developers lease malware to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share the proceeds with the developers. The article gives a frequently reported 70/30 profit split as an example, not as a Conti-specific adjudicated fact. [SRC-003]

Conti is described as a “notorious RaaS operation” that used double extortion and had apparent ties to other malware organizations, particularly TrickBot. [SRC-003] Rewards for Justice describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked RaaS group targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. This is an official government assessment or characterization, not a judicial finding established by the sources reviewed here. [SRC-001]

The reported operating model allowed developers to concentrate on malware development while affiliates or other third parties handled access and intrusions. CIS further describes initial-access brokers as entities that can sell established access to victim environments, thereby reducing the need for the ransomware organization to obtain access itself. [SRC-003]

### Extortion and victim impact

Rewards for Justice states that Conti operators typically:

1. Stole victims’ files;
2. Encrypted servers and workstations;
3. Directed victims to an online portal for ransom negotiations; and
4. Threatened to sell or publish stolen data if payment was not made. [SRC-001]

The same source states that Conti was first detected in 2019 and was used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations affecting more than 400 organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States. These figures are presented as government-source assertions and are not independently verified by the other benchmark sources. [SRC-001]

The Department of Justice states that Conti ransomware affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and elsewhere. The difference between the DOJ’s “more than 900” figure and Rewards for Justice’s “more than 400 organizations worldwide” figure is not explained in the sources and may reflect different counting methods, time periods, or definitions. [SRC-001][SRC-004]

---

## 2. What the Conti leaks exposed about internal structure

### Timing and contents of the disclosures

Rapid7 reports that the @ContiLeaks account released a trove of Conti chat logs on February 27, 2022, following Conti’s public support for the Russian government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The first reported archive contained approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. Some messages were encrypted and unreadable, so the available material was necessarily incomplete. [SRC-002]

Additional material reportedly included:

- Internal communications;
- Screenshots of tools and a Conti control panel;
- Discussions of exploits and malware design;
- Usernames and passwords;
- Alleged Conti command-and-control and storage-server details;
- Phishing templates; and
- An alleged ransomware source-code file. [SRC-002]

Rapid7 cautioned against accessing remote infrastructure using the leaked credentials or server information. The source also said the scale of the disclosure suggested that the leaker was likely either a senior member of Conti or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. This is a source assessment, not a confirmed identification. [SRC-002]

### Departments and personnel functions

CIS, summarizing reporting on the leaks, states that Conti divided its operations into business units and assigned personnel distinct roles, including:

- Coders;
- Testers;
- Administrators;
- Reverse engineers; and
- Penetration testers or hackers.

Spamming functions were reportedly contracted outside the organization. CIS also reports that the different units had their own budgets, although units could borrow money from one another. [SRC-003]

A Conti insider reportedly estimated that the group employed more than 60 people, mostly coders and testers, in July 2021. CIS presents this as an insider estimate, and notes that staffing levels changed, including after internal security breaches. [SRC-003]

### Evidence of corporate-style operations

The leaked chats reportedly included:

- Interviews for prospective operators;
- Coding exercises;
- Salary negotiations;
- Out-of-office messages;
- Payments for services;
- Product-development discussions; and
- Internal gossip. [SRC-002]

These details support the public description of Conti as more than a loosely connected group of operators. They suggest a division of labor resembling a software company or other commercial enterprise. Rapid7 specifically assessed that Conti “operated much like a software company,” based on discussions about features, encryption problems, endpoint-detection products, and malware development. [SRC-002]

CIS similarly characterizes the leaks as unusually direct evidence of the commercialization of cybercrime, including recruitment, finance, accounting, negotiation, and technical development functions. [SRC-003]

### Product development and operational improvement

Reported leak material indicated efforts to improve the ransomware product and its ability to evade security controls. Examples included:

- Acquiring a valid Cobalt Strike license;
- Paying for security and antivirus products so testers could evaluate the ransomware;
- Refocusing reverse engineers on Windows 11; and
- Testing endpoint-detection products to develop evasion techniques. [SRC-002][SRC-003]

Rapid7 also reports evidence of phishing activity, malicious-document logistics, and efforts to deliver ransomware without triggering dynamic analysis. A leaked control-panel screenshot reportedly displayed compromised hosts and information about operating systems, antivirus products, user rights, and infected assets. [SRC-002]

### Post-leak fragmentation and operational status

CIS reports that, after the leaks, the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, potentially improving mobility and law-enforcement evasion. It also reports that Conti’s leak and negotiation infrastructure shut down approximately one month later. [SRC-003]

Rapid7’s contemporaneous assessment was more cautious: it reported that Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure on March 2, 2022, but observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9 and assessed that Conti remained active and significant. [SRC-002]

These accounts are best understood as describing different stages of a transition rather than conclusively proving a single, clean shutdown date.

---

## 3. Public attribution, aliases, and law-enforcement records

### Publicly identified aliases

Rewards for Justice states that the online aliases below are believed to be linked to Conti:

- “Target”
- “Reshaev”
- “Professor”
- “Tramp”
- “Dandis” [SRC-001]

The same page identifies Wizard Spider as another name for Conti and lists Russia as an associated location. [SRC-001]

The wording “believed to be linked” indicates an attribution assessment rather than a court-established identity mapping. The benchmark sources do not provide sufficient evidence to identify the real-world individuals behind those aliases.

### Defendants named in DOJ records

The DOJ’s Conti Ransomware page identifies the following defendants in case **3:23-CR-00092**:

- Maksim Galochkin;
- Maksim Rudenskiy;
- Mikhail Tsarev; and
- Andrey Zhuykov. [SRC-004]

DOJ states that these defendants were charged in September 2023 with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, for their alleged roles in the Conti ransomware conspiracy. [SRC-004]

The same page identifies **Oleksii Lytvynenko** in case **3:23-CR-00088**. DOJ states that he was charged in November 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti ransomware. The page further states that, in June 2026, he pleaded guilty to Count 2 of the indictment, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. [SRC-004]

### Limits of the alias-to-defendant linkage

The sources establish two separate public records:

1. Rewards for Justice links five online aliases to Conti; and
2. DOJ identifies five named defendants in Conti-related criminal cases. [SRC-001][SRC-004]

However, the reviewed benchmark material does **not** establish that Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko used any of the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis.” No alias-to-defendant mapping should therefore be inferred.

Likewise, the sources do not establish that every person associated with one of the listed aliases was among the defendants named by DOJ.

---

## 4. Assessment of the evidence

### Strongly supported by the benchmark sources

- Conti was publicly described as a ransomware-as-a-service operation. [SRC-001][SRC-003]
- Wizard Spider was identified as another name for Conti. [SRC-001]
- Conti used or was associated with double-extortion practices. [SRC-001][SRC-003]
- The ContiLeaks disclosures included internal chats and operational material. [SRC-002][SRC-003]
- The leaks described recruitment, technical roles, product development, and operational coordination. [SRC-002][SRC-003]
- Rewards for Justice publicly linked five aliases to Conti. [SRC-001]
- DOJ publicly identified five defendants in Conti-related cases and described the charges against them. [SRC-004]

### Allegations, assessments, or uncertain points

- Conti’s alleged linkage to the Russian government is an official government characterization. [SRC-001]
- The identity and position of the ContiLeaks source are uncertain. [SRC-002]
- The reported FSB funding-related conversation is based on leaked chat material and is not independently verified in the reviewed source. [SRC-002]
- Staffing figures, business-unit descriptions, and some financial details rely on leaked material or insider reporting. [SRC-002][SRC-003]
- The precise relationship between the Conti brand and successor or rebranded groups is not fully established by these sources. [SRC-003]
- No reviewed source maps the listed Conti aliases to the DOJ defendants. [SRC-001][SRC-004]

---

## Source index

- **SRC-001** — *Conti - Rewards For Justice*, Rewards for Justice.
- **SRC-002** — *Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked*, Rapid7.
- **SRC-003** — *The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization*, Center for Internet Security.
- **SRC-004** — *Conti Ransomware*, U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee.

Rapid7 specifically assessed that Conti “operated much like a software company,” based on discussions about features, encryption problems, endpoint-detection products, and malware development. [SRC-002]

CIS similarly characterizes the leaks as unusually direct evidence of the commercialization of cybercrime, including recruitment, finance, accounting, negotiation, and technical development functions. [SRC-003]

### Product development and operational improvement

Reported leak material indicated efforts to improve the ransomware product and its ability to evade security controls. Examples included:

- Acquiring a valid Cobalt Strike license;
- Paying for security and antivirus products so testers could evaluate the ransomware;
- Refocusing reverse engineers on Windows 11; and
- Testing endpoint-detection products to develop evasion techniques. [SRC-002][SRC-003]

Rapid7 also reports evidence of phishing activity, malicious-document logistics, and efforts to deliver ransomware without triggering dynamic analysis. A leaked control-panel screenshot reportedly displayed compromised hosts and information about operating systems, antivirus products, user rights, and infected assets. [SRC-002]

### Post-leak fragmentation and operational status

CIS reports that, after the leaks, the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, potentially improving mobility and law-enforcement evasion. It also reports that Conti’s leak and negotiation infrastructure shut down approximately one month later. [SRC-003]

Rapid7’s contemporaneous assessment was more cautious: it reported that Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure on March 2, 2022, but observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9 and assessed that Conti remained active and significant. [SRC-002]

These accounts are best understood as describing different stages of a transition rather than conclusively proving a single, clean shutdown date.

## 3. Public attribution, aliases, and law-enforcement records

### Publicly identified aliases

Rewards for Justice states that the online aliases below are believed to be linked to Conti:

- “Target”
- “Reshaev”
- “Professor”
- “Tramp”
- “Dandis” [SRC-001]

The same page identifies Wizard Spider as another name for Conti and lists Russia as an associated location. [SRC-001]

The wording “believed to be linked” indicates an attribution assessment rather than a court-established identity mapping. The benchmark sources do not provide sufficient evidence to identify the real-world individuals behind those aliases.

### Defendants named in DOJ records

The DOJ’s Conti Ransomware page identifies the following defendants in case **3:23-CR-00092**:

- Maksim Galochkin;
- Maksim Rudenskiy;
- Mikhail Tsarev; and
- Andrey Zhuykov. [SRC-004]

DOJ states that these defendants were charged in September 2023 with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, for their alleged roles in the Conti ransomware conspiracy. [SRC-004]

The same page identifies **Oleksii Lytvynenko** in case **3:23-CR-00088**. DOJ states that he was charged in November 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti ransomware. The page further states that, in June 2026, he pleaded guilty to Count 2 of the indictment, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. [SRC-004]

### Limits of the alias-to-defendant linkage

The sources establish two separate public records:

1. Rewards for Justice links five online aliases to Conti; and
2. DOJ identifies five named defendants in Conti-related criminal cases. [SRC-001][SRC-004]

However, the reviewed benchmark material does **not** establish that Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko used any of the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis.” No alias-to-defendant mapping should therefore be inferred.

Likewise, the sources do not establish that every person associated with one of the listed aliases was among the defendants named by DOJ.

## 4. Assessment of the evidence

### Strongly supported by the benchmark sources

- Conti was publicly described as a ransomware-as-a-service operation. [SRC-001][SRC-003]
- Wizard Spider was identified as another name for Conti. [SRC-001]
- Conti used or was associated with double-extortion practices. [SRC-001][SRC-003]
- The ContiLeaks disclosures included internal chats and operational material. [SRC-002][SRC-003]
- The leaks described recruitment, technical roles, product development, and operational coordination. [SRC-002][SRC-003]
- Rewards for Justice publicly linked five aliases to Conti. [SRC-001]
- DOJ publicly identified five defendants in Conti-related cases and described the charges against them. [SRC-004]

### Allegations, assessments, or uncertain points

- Conti’s alleged linkage to the Russian government is an official government characterization. [SRC-001]
- The identity and position of the ContiLeaks source are uncertain. [SRC-002]
- The reported FSB funding-related conversation is based on leaked chat material and is not independently verified in the reviewed source. [SRC-002]
- Staffing figures, business-unit descriptions, and some financial details rely on leaked material or insider reporting. [SRC-002][SRC-003]
- The precise relationship between the Conti brand and successor or rebranded groups is not fully established by these sources. [SRC-003]
- No reviewed source maps the listed Conti aliases to the DOJ defendants. [SRC-001][SRC-004]
